analysis.one_liner: Tightens the federal revenue cap on for-profit colleges and cuts off military and veterans' education aid to schools that fail it.
analysis.headline: Maxine Waters' bill to tighten the 90/10 rule and cut off Pentagon and veterans' education aid to for-profit colleges that fail it received no cosponsors, no committee action, and never came to a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets a for-profit college collect up to 90% of its revenue from federal student aid. This bill would have tightened that to 85%, counting money from any federal program—including Pentagon and veterans' benefits—against that cap, so a school could not survive on federal dollars alone. It also would have required the Education Department to tell the Defense and Veterans Affairs Departments whenever a for-profit school lost federal aid eligibility, and cut off military and GI Bill education payments to that school. The bill never received a single cosponsor, never got a committee hearing or markup, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and service members who attend or are recruited by for-profit colleges. For-profit schools have historically relied on federal student aid and GI Bill benefits for most of their revenue, and veterans have been heavily recruited because those dollars count toward the school's 'non-federal' share under the old rule. By requiring schools to draw at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources and by cutting off Defense and VA education payments to schools that fail the test, the bill would have reduced the incentive to enroll students—especially veterans—into high-priced, low-quality programs funded by taxpayer money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students, service members, and veterans using federal education aid

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 90/10 rule with an 85/15 rule: a for-profit college must derive at least 15% of its revenue from sources other than federal funds, rather than the current 10% [S2].
Counts money from any federal program—not just Title IV student aid—against that cap, closing the loophole under which Pentagon and VA education dollars did not count [S2].
Requires the Education Department to notify the Defense Department and VA when a for-profit institution loses federal student aid eligibility and when it regains it [S2].
Makes a for-profit institution ineligible to receive Defense Department or VA educational assistance for as long as it remains ineligible for federal student aid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their shareholders, whose schools would lose access to federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill benefits if they could not draw at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources. Schools that lose eligibility would have to shrink, restructure, or close, and their current students would need to transfer to finish their programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves one carve-out: the monthly housing stipend under the Post-9/11 GI Bill does not count as a federal fund, so schools could still count that money toward their required non-federal share, preserving some incentive to target veterans' housing benefits [S3].

A school that fails the 85/15 test would be cut off from federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill payments entirely, leaving enrolled students scrambling to transfer rather than offering a graduated path [S2].
Tighter revenue requirements could push some career and technical schools to raise tuition or cut programs for students who pay out of pocket, in order to make the non-federal share [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff favors students and taxpayers: requiring schools to earn 15% of revenue from non-federal sources is a direct check on business models built almost entirely on federal aid, and cutting off Pentagon and VA payments to ineligible schools stops federal education money from flowing to programs that fail one federal eligibility test. The main costs fall on the for-profit college companies themselves, though a hard cutoff also leaves enrolled students without a transition path, and the housing-stipend carve-out weakens the protection for veterans—the very group the bill is most meant to shield.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three committees and two subcommittees on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever acted on it; it received no cosponsors and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA) introduced the bill on June 5, 2019 [S1].
It was referred to the Education and Labor, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs Committees the same day [S5].

It was sent to the Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel (June 6, 2019) and the Veterans' Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity (June 25, 2019), where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party [S4].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill advancing [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college operators, who kept the looser 90/10 rule and continued to collect federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill dollars—including the housing stipend carve-out—without the tighter revenue test or the aid cutoff.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the For-Profit Fraud Act to tighten the 90/10 rule and cut off Defense and VA education aid to for-profit schools that fail it

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors from either party, so neither caucus visibly backed it, and no committee or floor vote ever revealed where members stood.

industries.note: The bill targets schools that draw most of their revenue from federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill benefits, and cuts off Defense and VA education payments to any school that loses federal aid eligibility. Its interest in blocking or weakening the bill runs against students and taxpayers, since the rule change exists to limit schools funded almost entirely by federal money.
